15950:
Picture your actual skin for a moment. If your skin were very thick — like leather or armor — sharp things like needles or thorns would have a much harder time piercing through it and hurting you. You'd be physically protected.

Now take that same idea and apply it to your emotions. When we say a person is thick-skinned, we mean their emotional "skin" is like that thick armor. Hurtful words, harsh criticism, insults, mockery, or rejection don't easily pierce them — these things don't wound them deeply or upset them greatly.

In short: a thick-skinned person is someone who is not easily hurt, offended, or bothered by what others say or think about them.
What Being Thick-Skinned Actually Looks Like

A thick-skinned person can:

  • Receive sharp criticism without falling apart or getting defensive
  • Hear an insult and shrug it off rather than stewing over it for days
  • Face repeated rejection and keep going without losing confidence
  • Work in an environment where people are blunt, harsh, or even unkind — and still function well
  • Hear very negative feedback about their work and use it constructively, rather than feeling crushed

They don't ruminate. They don't take every comment personally. They have a kind of internal shield.

Think of two different people standing in the rain of criticism:

  • The thin-skinned person gets soaked. Every drop hits hard. They feel every word deeply.
  • The thick-skinned person is wearing a thick raincoat. The rain still falls, but it slides off. They notice it, but it doesn't drench them.

This is why "thick-skinned" is such a powerful and accurate description. The metaphor is doing real work.

Being thick-skinned is not an on/off switch. It exists on a scale.

  • Someone can be extremely thick-skinned — barely rattled by even the harshest of attacks.
  • Someone can be moderately thick-skinned — able to handle routine criticism well, but still hurt by deeply personal attacks.
  • Someone can be not thick-skinned at all (i.e., thin-skinned) — upset by even mild, well-meaning feedback.

Also, a person might be thick-skinned in one area of their life but not another. A comedian might be very thick-skinned about jokes at their expense on stage, but still sensitive about criticism of their parenting.
Is Being Thick-Skinned Good or Bad?

This is where it gets interesting — it depends entirely on context and degree.

When it's seen as a strength (positive connotation):

Certain roles in life genuinely demand thick skin:

  • Politicians who face public attack every day
  • Artists or writers whose work is constantly judged and rejected
  • Salespeople who hear "no" dozens of times a day
  • Athletes who face jeering crowds
  • Leaders who must make unpopular decisions

In these situations, we admire thick-skinnedness. We say things like, "You need to be thick-skinned to survive in this industry." It signals resilience, mental strength, and the ability to keep moving forward under pressure.

When it's seen as a flaw (negative connotation):

If someone is too thick-skinned, it can mean they have become:

  • Unempathetic — they don't just shrug off unfair attacks; they also fail to respond appropriately to valid, caring feedback.
  • Callous — so used to hardship that they've lost sensitivity toward others too.
  • Arrogant or dismissive — using "I'm thick-skinned" as an excuse to ignore legitimate concerns.

There is a meaningful difference between being thick-skinned in a healthy way (resilience) and being thick-skinned to a fault (emotional unavailability or dismissiveness).

Being thick-skinned does not mean:

  • The person feels nothing. They are not robots. They may still feel a sting — they simply don't let it derail them or linger long.
  • The person is aggressive or cold. A thick-skinned person can be warm, kind, and emotionally open. Their shield is for incoming criticism, not a wall against all human connection.
  • The person is right for ignoring all criticism. Being too thick-skinned can mean missing important signals that you need to change or improve.

The direct opposite is thin-skinned — someone who is highly sensitive to criticism or negative opinions, easily hurt or offended, and who takes things very personally. Understanding the opposite word sharpens your understanding of the original:

  • "She is so thin-skinned that even a gentle suggestion makes her defensive."
  • "He is thick-skinned enough to read every negative review of his book and not lose sleep."
Example Sentences (to see it in action)

1. "If you want to be a stand-up comedian, you need to be thick-skinned — audiences can be brutal."
  2. "She's thick-skinned when it comes to professional feedback, but don't say anything about her cooking."
  3. "Years of rejection in the publishing world made him thick-skinned."
  4. "A good politician has to be thick-skinned — the press will scrutinize every decision."
  5. "I admire how thick-skinned she is; someone said her presentation was terrible and she just smiled and asked what she could improve."

Thick-skinned = emotionally resilient; not easily hurt, offended, or discouraged by criticism, insults, or rejection.

It is generally a compliment — a quality that helps people endure difficult environments — but taken too far, it can shade into insensitivity or arrogance.

A thicket is a dense, tangled mass of wild plants — such as bushes, shrubs, brambles, or small trees — all growing so closely packed together that it becomes very difficult, or even impossible, to walk through them easily.

Think of it this way: if a single bush is like one person standing alone, a thicket is like a crowd of people standing so tightly together that you can barely squeeze between them. The plants in a thicket are not neatly arranged — they are wild, messy, and interlocked, with branches and stems crossing over each other.

Three things define a thicket:

1. Density — The plants are packed tightly. There is very little open space between them. This is the most important quality of a thicket.

2. Difficulty of passage — Because the plants are so dense and tangled, a person or animal trying to pass through them gets blocked, scratched, or slowed down. You might need to push branches aside, duck under them, or even use a tool like a knife or a stick to cut your way through.

3. Wildness — A thicket is not a garden or a neatly trimmed hedge. It grows on its own, in nature, without human control. You would typically find a thicket at the edge of a forest, along a riverbank, in an overgrown field, or in a woodland.
What Plants Make Up a Thicket?

A thicket is not made of just one type of plant. It is usually a mix of:

  • Shrubs (low, woody plants with many branches)
  • Brambles (thorny, tangled plants like blackberry or raspberry bushes)
  • Small trees (young or short trees)
  • Tall weeds and vines

The mix of these plants, all growing wildly on top of and around each other, is what creates that characteristic dense, hard-to-enter tangle.

A thicket is relatively small and localized — it occupies a patch or cluster, not a vast area. This is important because it helps you tell a thicket apart from a forest.

Think of it on a scale like this:

  • A single bush → just one plant
  • A thicket → a dense patch of many plants clustered together (could be the size of a room, a house, or a small field)
  • A forest → a vast, wide area of trees stretching for miles

A thicket fits in the middle — bigger than a single plant, but much smaller and more localized than a forest.

Since you want a complete understanding, it helps to know how "thicket" differs from words that might seem similar:

  • Grove — A small, pleasant group of trees with open space between them. A grove is easy and inviting to walk through. A thicket is not. Think of an olive grove or an orange grove — airy and accessible.
  • Forest / Wood — Much larger than a thicket. A forest is a vast area. A thicket is just a dense patch.
  • Undergrowth — This refers to low plants growing beneath taller trees. A thicket can exist on its own, out in the open, not necessarily under trees.
  • Brush / Scrub — These words also describe low, wild plant growth, but they don't carry the same strong emphasis on density and difficulty of passage that "thicket" does.

"Thicket" is also used figuratively — that is, to describe a complicated, confusing, or tangled situation (not a physical place) that is very hard to navigate or get through, just like a real thicket is hard to walk through.

This figurative use is extremely common in writing and speech. Examples:

  • "The new lawyer found herself in a thicket of conflicting laws."
  • "The negotiation turned into a thicket of competing demands."
  • "He got lost in a thicket of bureaucratic paperwork."

In each case, the idea is the same: something is so dense, tangled, and confusing that it is very hard to find your way through it. The word "thicket" carries the feeling of being stuck, slowed down, and surrounded.

These will help you see the word in its natural habitat:

  • "The fox darted into the thicket and vanished from sight."
  • "We forced our way through a thicket of brambles to reach the stream."
  • "A dense thicket of thorny bushes grew along the old stone wall."
  • "The hunters lost the trail where the path disappeared into a dark thicket."

If you had to remember just one definition: A thicket is a dense, tangled, wild cluster of bushes, shrubs, or small trees so closely packed together that it is very difficult to pass through.

Everything else — the figurative uses, the comparisons to similar words, the sense of wildness and chaos — all flows from that core idea of something being thick, tangled, and hard to get through.
15952: To thieve means to steal — to take things that belong to someone else, without their permission, and with the intention of keeping those things. Simple as that. If someone is thieving, they are behaving like a thief.
The Key Character of This Word

Here is the most important thing to understand about "thieve": it almost always describes a habit, a pattern of behavior, or an ongoing act — not just a single, specific theft. This is what makes it subtly different from the word steal.

Think of it this way:

When you say "He stole my wallet," you are pointing at one specific act — one wallet, one moment.

When you say "He thieves," you are saying something about who he is and what he does repeatedly. You are describing a behavior that has become part of his character or routine.

So "thieve" paints a bigger picture of a person. It says: this is someone who steals, regularly, as a way of life or habit.

"Thieve" is mostly used as an intransitive verb, which means it often does not need a direct object after it. You don't always need to say what was stolen — the word is complete on its own.

For example:

  • "He had been thieving for years before he was caught."
  • "She thieves to feed her family."
  • "They were found thieving in the market."

Notice that none of these sentences need to name the stolen object. The focus is on the act and habit of stealing itself.

That said, you can use an object with it on occasion:

  • "He thieved money from the shop."

But this kind of sentence is less common. When people want to talk about a specific object being stolen, they usually prefer the word steal ("He stole money from the shop").

FormExample
Base formthieve
He/she/it (present)thieves
Past tensethieved
Past participlethieved
Ongoing action (-ing)thieving

⚠️ One thing to watch carefully: The word thieves has two completely different identities in English.

  • Thieves (noun) = more than one thief → "A gang of thieves robbed the bank."
  • Thieves (verb) = the present tense of "thieve" when used with he/she/it → "She thieves whenever she gets the chance."

The spelling is identical. Only the context tells you which one it is.

"Thieving" is also very commonly used as an adjective — a describing word — placed before a noun to label someone as a habitual thief, often with strong emotion (anger, frustration, or even humor).

  • "Keep your eyes on that thieving rascal."
  • "The thieving employees had been stealing from the company for months."
  • "Get away from my apples, you thieving little monkey!"

This is a vivid, punchy way to use the word and you'll come across it often in everyday speech, books, and films.

Steal — The closest word to "thieve." The two are nearly identical in meaning, but steal is far more common in everyday language and works better when you're talking about one specific act of theft. Thieve is slightly more formal, slightly more literary, and leans toward describing repeated behavior.

Pilfer — To steal small, petty things, usually repeatedly — like office supplies, small change, or food. "She pilfered snacks from the break room every day."

Filch — Very similar to pilfer. Small-scale, sneaky theft. "The boy filched a coin from his mother's purse."

Purloin — A formal or humorous word for steal. You'll mostly see it in older literature or when someone wants to sound deliberately old-fashioned or witty. "He purloined the documents from the minister's desk."

Nick / Lift / Swipe — Informal, casual words for steal. "Someone nicked my umbrella." / "He lifted a watch from the display case." / "She swiped a fry from my plate."

Among all these, thieve sits closest to steal, but with that extra shade of meaning — habitual, repeated, or characteristic dishonest behavior.
The Register: When and Where Is This Word Used?

"Thieve" is not a word you'll hear in every casual conversation. It lives mostly in written English, literature, journalism, and slightly formal speech. An average person on the street is more likely to say "he steals" than "he thieves."

However, "thieving" (the -ing adjective form) is quite common in everyday emotional speech, especially when someone is angry — "You thieving liar!"

To thieve is to steal — but with a particular emphasis on doing so as a habit or repeated pattern of behavior. It's mostly intransitive (doesn't need an object). Its -ing form, thieving, is widely used as a colorful adjective to describe someone as a habitual thief. It's slightly more formal than steal, and you'll meet it most often in writing, literature, or emotional outbursts. Knowing the difference between the noun thieves (plural of thief) and the verb thieves (he/she/it thieves) is an important detail to hold onto.

A thimble is a small, hard, cap-like shield that you slip over the tip of your finger — almost always the middle finger — to protect it while you are sewing by hand.

When you sew by hand, you have to push a needle through fabric over and over again. The blunt end of the needle (the "eye" end) presses hard against your fingertip with every push. Without protection, this quickly becomes painful, and over time it can break the skin. A thimble sits between your fingertip and the needle, taking all that pressure so your skin doesn't have to.

Picture a tiny cup or dome, roughly the size of your own fingertip. It is:

  • Open at the bottom — this is where your finger goes in.
  • Closed and rounded at the top — this is the surface that actually touches the needle.
  • Small — typically about 2–3 cm tall and just wide enough to fit snugly over a fingertip.
  • Covered in tiny dents (dimples or pits) all over its outer surface. These are not just decoration. They serve a purpose: they grip the smooth metal end of the needle and stop it from slipping sideways when you push. Without these dimples, the needle would slide off and could stab your finger anyway.

The most traditional material is metal — usually steel, brass, or silver. Metal is ideal because it is hard enough to block a needle completely. However, thimbles are also made from:

  • Leather — softer and more flexible, preferred by some tailors and leatherworkers.
  • Rubber or silicone — more modern, comfortable, and grippy.
  • Bone, ivory, glass, or ceramic — mostly in older times or as decorative and collectible items.

A metal thimble gives the best protection; a leather thimble gives more "feel" of the fabric. The right choice depends on the person and the job.

You push the thimble onto the tip of your middle finger (on whichever hand you use to push the needle). It should fit snugly — not so tight that it cuts off circulation, not so loose that it falls off. Then, when you push the needle through fabric, you press the needle's blunt end against the closed top of the thimble, using it like a tiny pushing platform. The hard surface of the thimble does the work your soft skin cannot.

This is especially useful when sewing through thick or tough materials like denim, canvas, leather, or multiple layers of fabric stacked together.
A second, less common meaning — in rope and metalwork

In a completely different context — particularly in sailing, rigging, and engineering — a thimble refers to a small, grooved metal ring or loop, usually teardrop-shaped or oval, that is fitted inside a looped end of a rope or wire cable.

When a rope forms a loop (called an "eye"), the thimble sits inside that loop to give it a rigid, smooth shape. It prevents the rope from bending too sharply at the loop, and it protects the rope from being cut or worn down by friction when a hook, shackle, or another rope is attached to it. Without the thimble, the rope would fray and weaken at that spot over time.

So in this sense, the thimble is not about sewing at all — it is a protective lining for a rope's eye. The idea is similar though: something hard placed between a soft material and a source of pressure or wear.

Because a thimble is so tiny, the word is also used informally to describe an extremely small quantity of something, especially a liquid. If someone says "I'll just have a thimbleful of brandy," they mean just a tiny drop — barely any at all. This usage is simply borrowed from the small size of the object itself.
The thimble as a cultural object

The thimble has a long history as a collectible item. Many people collect thimbles as a hobby — gathering them in different metals, designs, sizes, and from different countries. Collectors often display them on special stands or in glass cases. Fancy thimbles can be made of silver or gold, decorated with engravings, gemstones, or painted enamel scenes.

The thimble is also widely recognized as one of the classic playing pieces (tokens) from the board game Monopoly, where it was used as a small metal game piece from the game's early days (though it was later retired from the standard set in 2013).
A thimble is a small, hard, dimpled cap worn on a fingertip to protect it from needle pricks while sewing — and by extension, any small protective ring used to guard a rope's loop from wear.

Before you can understand the idiom, you need to picture a wedge — a simple, ancient tool shaped like a triangle. One end is razor-thin, almost like a knife's edge. The other end is wide and thick. Wedges are used to split things apart: you press the thin end into a small crack in a piece of wood or rock, and then hammer it in. As it goes deeper, the thicker part forces the crack to open wider and wider until, eventually, the whole thing splits open completely.

Here is what matters: the thin end goes in easily, almost without resistance. But it brings the thick end along with it — and that is what does the real damage.

When someone says that something is "the thin end of the wedge," they mean:

This thing looks small and harmless right now, but allowing it will open the door to much bigger, more serious, or more damaging things in the future.

The "thin end" is the small, seemingly innocent step. The "thick end" — which is implied but not always stated — is the serious consequence that will inevitably follow. The warning is: don't be fooled by how small or reasonable this first step looks, because it will lead somewhere much more significant.
The Tone: Almost Always a Warning

This idiom is nearly always used as a warning or as an expression of disapproval or concern. It carries a negative or cautious tone. You say it when you want to argue against allowing something, even if that something appears minor, because you believe it will set a dangerous precedent — meaning, once you allow it once, it becomes the starting point for allowing more and more.

You will rarely, if ever, hear this phrase used to celebrate or encourage something.

Example 1 — Workplace rules:
Imagine a company has a strict rule: no personal phone use during work hours. One employee asks: "Can I just check my phone for five minutes at lunch?" A strict manager might say:

"I'm sorry, but this is the thin end of the wedge. If I allow it for you, everyone will want it, and soon people will be on their phones all day."

The five-minute phone check is the thin end. Total loss of productivity is the thick end.

Example 2 — Parenting:
A child asks to stay up 30 minutes past bedtime — just this once, because there's a good film on. A parent might think:

"If I say yes tonight, that's the thin end of the wedge. Next week there will be another reason, and the week after that another, until bedtime means nothing."

Example 3 — Politics and law:
In political debate, this phrase is used all the time. If a government proposes a small new tax or a minor restriction on some freedom, opponents will often say:

"This may look like a tiny measure today, but it's the thin end of the wedge. Once governments get a foot in the door, they always push further."

Example 4 — Everyday life:
Your friend asks you to cover for them at work just this once. You might hesitate and think:

"I don't want to do it. This feels like the thin end of the wedge — if I do it now, they'll expect it every time something comes up."
The Core Idea: The Slippery Slope

You may have heard of a "slippery slope" — the idea that one small step leads inevitably to larger and larger consequences, like a ball rolling down a hill that keeps gathering speed. "The thin end of the wedge" is closely related to this idea, but with a specific emphasis: the focus is on how deceptively harmless the starting point looks. It is the smallness and apparent innocence of the first step that makes the wedge so dangerous. If the first step looked scary or large, people would refuse it immediately. But because it's thin — because it looks fine — people let it in, and that is exactly the problem.
An Important Nuance: Can It Be an Exaggeration?

Yes. It is worth knowing that not every small concession actually leads to disaster. Sometimes people use "the thin end of the wedge" as an argument that is exaggerated or overly cautious. Critics of this kind of thinking sometimes call it a slippery slope fallacy — the mistake of assuming that one small step automatically leads to the worst outcome, when in reality, things can be controlled or stopped at any point.

So when you hear this phrase, understand that the person using it genuinely fears a chain of events, but they may or may not be right. The phrase describes their concern, not a guaranteed fact of what will happen.

• It is a noun phrase — it names a situation or an action.
  • It is used as the subject or object of a sentence.
  • Common patterns:
    • "This is the thin end of the wedge."
    • "Allowing X would be the thin end of the wedge."
    • "I see this as the thin end of the wedge."
    • "Beware — this is just the thin end of the wedge."

The phrase is primarily British English in origin and has been in use since at least the early-to-mid 1800s. It comes directly from the physical use of wedges in carpentry, stonecutting, and mining — trades where workers understood very well that the moment a wedge enters a crack, the splitting process has already begun. The phrase moved from the workshop into everyday language as a natural metaphor.

"The thin end of the wedge" means: a small, seemingly harmless step that is actually the beginning of a much larger and more serious process — and therefore something to be cautious about or refused, even if it looks innocent.

The next time you hear someone say it, you will know they are essentially saying: "Don't let this in, even though it looks small — it won't stay small."

Thin-skinned describes a person who gets hurt, offended, or upset very easily — especially when someone criticizes them, teases them, or says something negative about them or their work.

A thin-skinned person reacts more strongly than most people would to the same situation. What others might shrug off or laugh about, a thin-skinned person takes to heart and feels deeply wounded by.

The word is built on a simple, powerful image: your skin is your body's outer barrier — it protects what's inside.

  • If your skin is thick, it takes a lot to pierce through it. Things bounce off you. You can take a hit.
  • If your skin is thin, even a light touch breaks through. You feel every little poke. You're easy to hurt.

Now apply this to feelings and emotions: a thin-skinned person has a very thin emotional barrier. Criticism, mockery, or even a slightly negative comment cuts right through to them. They feel the pain deeply and quickly.

The opposite is thick-skinned — someone who can absorb criticism, brush off teasing, and stay unfazed by negative opinions. Where a thick-skinned person hears criticism and thinks "okay, noted," a thin-skinned person hears the same thing and feels personally attacked or devastated.

Thin-skinned people tend to:

  • Take criticism personally, even when it is meant to be constructive and helpful.
  • Overreact to teasing or jokes — they may feel humiliated or deeply hurt by something others intended lightly.
  • Become defensive quickly when their ideas, opinions, or work are challenged.
  • Dwell on negative comments long after the moment has passed.
  • Struggle to separate their work from their identity — so if you criticize what they did, they feel like you're criticizing who they are.
Thin-skinned is about receiving, not giving

This is an important distinction: thin-skinned is specifically about how a person handles negativity directed at them. It is not a word about how someone treats others. A thin-skinned person might actually be kind, generous, and calm in most situations — but the moment someone criticizes them or makes a joke at their expense, their emotional response is disproportionately large.

Thin-skinned is mildly critical or disapproving in tone. When you call someone thin-skinned, you're suggesting that they are too sensitive — that they need to develop more emotional resilience. It carries an implicit message: "You need to toughen up a little."

It is not an insult in the harshest sense, but it is not a compliment either. It is the kind of word used to describe someone's weakness in handling negative feedback or social friction.

Here are different situations where this word applies:

  1. A writer submits her short story. The editor gives thoughtful suggestions for improvement. She stops writing altogether because she feels crushed by the feedback. → She is thin-skinned about her writing.
  2. Friends are joking around. One friend makes a lighthearted comment about another's haircut. The second friend doesn't speak to anyone for the rest of the evening because he feels humiliated. → He is thin-skinned.
  3. A politician faces questions from journalists about a policy decision. Instead of engaging with the questions, he lashes out at the reporters and calls it an attack. → He is being thin-skinned.
  4. A manager gives her employee a small piece of constructive feedback in a private meeting. The employee becomes visibly upset and spends the whole next week believing her career is ruined. → She is thin-skinned.

• "You can't be thin-skinned in this job — clients will push back on your ideas all the time."
  • "Don't be so thin-skinned; she was just teasing you, not being mean."
  • "He's too thin-skinned to handle negative reviews, which is a problem for any public figure."
  • "Growing up, I was very thin-skinned, but over the years I've learned not to let criticism affect me so much."

• It does not mean someone is physically weak or fragile.
  • It does not mean someone is emotional in general. A thin-skinned person may be perfectly composed and confident — until criticism or mockery arrives.
  • It does not simply mean someone is empathetic or caring. Empathy is about feeling others' emotions; thin-skinned is about being excessively sensitive to how others' words and judgments land on you.
  • It does not mean someone is shy or introverted. A bold, outgoing person can absolutely be thin-skinned.
The key idea, summarized in one sentence
A thin-skinned person lacks the emotional armor to absorb criticism, teasing, or negative opinions without feeling disproportionately hurt, offended, or defensive.

A think piece is a written article or essay whose main job is not to report news, but to explore ideas. It asks the reader to slow down, consider a topic from a new angle, and — as the name suggests — think.

If a news article tells you what happened, a think piece asks what does it mean?, why does it matter?, or what should we make of all this?
What Makes It a Think Piece?

A think piece has a few key qualities that set it apart from other types of writing:

1. It goes beyond facts.
A news article might say: "A new study shows that people spend 4 hours a day on their phones." A think piece takes that same fact and digs into it: Is this making us lonelier? Are we losing the ability to be bored? What does this say about modern life?

2. The writer's perspective is front and centre.
Think pieces are not neutral. The writer has a point of view, an argument, or at least a strong angle. They are not just presenting information — they are interpreting it. This is what separates a think piece from a plain report or a Wikipedia entry.

3. It is meant to provoke thought, discussion, or debate.
The goal is not just to inform you — it is to stir something in you. You might finish reading one and find yourself nodding strongly, or fiercely disagreeing, or seeing something familiar in a totally new light. Either way, you are thinking.

4. It is usually tied to something current or culturally relevant.
Think pieces often appear when something big happens — a viral moment, a new film, a social movement, a scientific breakthrough, a political event. They ride the wave of public attention on a topic and try to add depth to the conversation.

To understand a think piece clearly, it helps to separate it from similar things:

  • Not a news article. A news article reports events — who, what, when, where. A think piece interprets events — why, what does it mean, what should we do.
  • Not a research paper. A research paper is academic, heavily sourced, and clinically neutral. A think piece is meant to be read by a general audience; it is conversational, personal, and opinionated.
  • Not a review. A film review tells you whether a film is good or bad. A think piece might use a film as a jumping-off point to talk about something bigger — gender roles in Hollywood, say, or how we deal with grief as a society.
  • Not an op-ed, exactly — though they are cousins. An op-ed (short for "opinion editorial") is a short, punchy opinion piece, usually with a clear call to action. A think piece tends to be longer, more exploratory, and more analytical. It sits with a question rather than immediately pushing a solution. The two terms, however, do overlap and are sometimes used interchangeably.

Think pieces are published in:

  • Newspapers and magazines — The New York Times, The Atlantic, The Guardian, Time, Vox, The New Yorker
  • Online media publications — many digital outlets publish them regularly
  • Newsletters and blogs written by journalists, academics, or public intellectuals

They are usually long-form — anywhere from 800 words to several thousand words — because they need the space to develop an idea properly.

Think pieces are written by journalists, cultural critics, academics, essayists, or anyone considered to have something insightful to say on a topic. The writer's credibility — whether from professional experience, lived experience, or expertise — matters a lot. When you read a think piece, you are not just reading about a topic; you are reading one person's mind working through a topic.

Imagine a famous actor quits social media after being harassed online.

  • A news article covers it: "Actor X deletes all social media accounts following harassment."
  • A think piece digs in: "Why do we demand constant access to celebrities — and what does it say about us that we punish them when they step back? This isn't just about one actor. It's about how social media has turned public figures into emotional punching bags, and how we all play a role in that."

The think piece uses the event as a doorway into a bigger, more complicated conversation.

It is worth knowing that the term think piece has also developed a mildly sarcastic edge in everyday language, especially online. People sometimes use it mockingly to describe articles that seem deep and thoughtful but are actually overblown, pretentious, or obsessed with trivial things. For example, someone might say: "There are already twelve think pieces about why that celebrity's haircut is a symbol of late capitalism."

This ironic use exists because the format became so popular that it got diluted — not every article that poses as a deep exploration actually has something genuinely insightful to say. So when people say think piece with a rolled eye, they mean an article that takes itself too seriously, or that finds grand meaning in things that do not really deserve it.

In serious, professional contexts, though, the term is still used neutrally and respectfully to describe thoughtful, analytical long-form writing.

A think piece is an article that uses a current event, trend, or cultural moment as a starting point to offer deep analysis, a strong perspective, and ideas that are meant to make the reader reflect and think — going well beyond simply reporting what happened.

To think straight means to think clearly, logically, and in an organized way. When you think straight, your mind is working properly — you can focus on a problem, reason through it step by step, and arrive at sensible conclusions without getting confused or going in circles.

When you cannot think straight, your mind feels cloudy, jumbled, or scattered. Your thoughts don't connect properly. You may struggle to make decisions, understand simple things, or make basic sense of what's happening around you.

The word "straight" is the key to unlocking this expression. Think of a straight line — it travels directly from Point A to Point B. It doesn't curve, wander, or zigzag. It is clear, direct, and clean.

Now apply that image to your thinking. When your thoughts move in a straight line, they flow logically: one idea leads to the next, each step makes sense, and you reach your conclusion without getting lost. That is thinking straight.

When you can't think straight, your thoughts are like a tangled ball of string — knotted, curved everywhere, with no clear path forward.

Grammatically, "think" is the verb and "straight" is an adverb modifying how you think. This makes "think straight" a verb phrase (verb + adverb).

This is an important point: "straight" here is not an adjective describing you as a person. It describes the manner in which you are thinking.

The expression appears most commonly in these forms:

  • can't think straight — "I'm so tired I can't think straight."
  • couldn't think straight — "She was so shocked she couldn't think straight."
  • unable to think straight — "He was too angry to think straight."
  • think straight (positive) — "Let me sit down quietly so I can think straight."
  • need to think straight — "I need a moment alone so I can think straight about this."

Important note: The negative form ("can't think straight") is far more common in everyday conversation than the positive form. People typically use this expression to describe a moment when normal thinking has broken down, rather than to describe normal functioning. This is natural — we tend to notice and comment on disruption more than on things working as they should.
What Stops a Person from Thinking Straight?

This expression is almost always linked to a specific cause — something that is interfering with clear thought. Common causes include:

  • Exhaustion or sleep deprivation — "I've been awake for 20 hours. I can't think straight."
  • Stress or anxiety — "She was so worried about the exam she couldn't think straight."
  • Emotional overwhelm — grief, fear, or intense anger can completely cloud the mind.
  • Alcohol or drugs — substances are classic disruptors of straight thinking.
  • Illness or pain — when your body suffers, your mind often follows.
  • Extreme hunger — "I haven't eaten all day. I can barely think straight."
  • Loud noise or too many distractions — "The music is so loud I can't think straight in here."
  • Information overload — being given too much at once can make your thinking scramble.

Notice that in all these cases, the person is not permanently impaired — something temporary is getting in the way. The expression almost always implies that once the disruption is removed (you sleep, calm down, eat, or step outside), you will be able to think straight again.

Here are natural examples so you can feel how native speakers use this expression:

  1. "I need a cup of coffee before I can think straight in the morning."
  2. "Stop shouting at me! I can't think straight when you do that."
  3. "After the accident, she was so shaken she couldn't think straight for days."
  4. "Take a break. Go for a walk. Come back when you can think straight."
  5. "He hadn't slept in two days — there was no way he could think straight."
  6. "I'm so nervous about tonight that I can barely think straight."
  7. "Give me a moment of silence. I just need to think straight."
  8. "Once the fever broke, he could finally think straight again."

"Think straight" is an informal, everyday expression. You will hear it in casual conversation, in novels, in films, and in everyday writing. It is used widely in both American English and British English without any regional restriction.

It is not slang — it is perfectly acceptable in moderately formal writing too, though in a very formal or academic context, you might prefer "think clearly" or "reason clearly" instead.
How It Differs from Similar Expressions

Understanding nearby expressions will sharpen your grasp of this one:

  • "Think clearly" — almost identical in meaning; "think straight" is slightly more vivid and informal because of its visual metaphor.
  • "Think rationally" — this places more emphasis on logic specifically, whereas "think straight" emphasizes being free from mental fog in general.
  • "Keep a clear head" — similar idea, but this focuses on maintaining clarity over time, often in a challenging situation (e.g., in a crisis).
  • "Get your head straight" — this means to sort out your confused or troubled thoughts, often with an emotional component. It implies something emotional needs to be resolved before you can think properly.
  • "Collect your thoughts" — this means to gather and organize your ideas before speaking or acting; it's about preparation, not about a clouded mind.

"Think straight" is not about intelligence. It is about the temporary ability to function mentally under present conditions. A brilliant scientist who hasn't slept in 40 hours cannot think straight. A child who has rested, eaten, and is calm can think straight. The expression is always about circumstances affecting the mind, never about how smart someone is.

"Think straight" means to think clearly and logically without confusion — and when someone "can't think straight," something (tiredness, stress, emotion, or distraction) is temporarily blocking their mind from working in that calm, focused, step-by-step way.

A think tank is an organization whose main job is to research complex problems and produce ideas, recommendations, and solutions — especially on topics like government policy, economics, foreign affairs, national security, technology, or social issues.

The word "tank" here is used in the old sense of a contained space for deep thought — imagine a room (a "tank") filled with smart, focused thinkers. A think tank is essentially that: a dedicated space where experts think hard about big problems.
What a Think Tank Actually Does

Think tanks employ researchers, analysts, economists, former politicians, retired military officers, scientists, and other experts. These people spend their time:

  • Studying problems — for example, "Why is inflation rising?" or "How should a country respond to cyberattacks?"
  • Analyzing data and evidence — reading reports, running their own studies, reviewing history
  • Writing papers and reports — called policy papers, white papers, or briefs, these are detailed documents explaining what they found
  • Making recommendations — telling governments, companies, or the public what they should do based on their research
  • Hosting conferences and debates — bringing experts together to discuss issues publicly
  • Advising decision-makers — sometimes their researchers go on TV, testify before parliament or congress, or directly advise ministers and presidents

Think tanks do not implement policies themselves — they don't pass laws or run programs. They influence those who do. Their power lies in ideas, not execution.

Think tanks are typically funded by one or more of the following:

  • Governments — some are partly or fully funded by the state
  • Corporations and businesses — companies fund research that may benefit their industry
  • Wealthy individuals and philanthropists — private donors with ideological or intellectual interests
  • Foundations — large charitable organizations like the Ford Foundation or Open Society Foundations
  • Membership fees and donations — from the public or institutions

Funding matters because it can shape what topics a think tank researches and what conclusions it tends to reach. A think tank funded by oil companies, for example, may produce research that is more skeptical of climate regulations. This doesn't mean their research is always wrong — but it's something aware readers keep in mind.
Think Tanks Are Not Neutral — They Often Have a Political Leaning

Many think tanks lean in a particular ideological direction:

  • Conservative/right-leaning think tanks tend to favor free markets, lower taxes, strong military, and less government regulation. Example: The Heritage Foundation (USA), Policy Exchange (UK).
  • Liberal/left-leaning think tanks tend to favor social programs, environmental regulation, workers' rights, and government intervention in the economy. Example: Center for American Progress (USA), Institute for Public Policy Research (UK).
  • Centrist or non-partisan think tanks try to be ideologically neutral and focus purely on evidence-based research. Example: Brookings Institution (USA), Chatham House (UK).

Some think tanks are openly ideological; others claim to be strictly neutral. As a reader, it's worth knowing a think tank's general orientation before accepting their conclusions at face value.
Think Tanks vs. Other Similar Organizations

Since think tanks can be confused with similar-sounding bodies, here's how they differ:

  • Universities also do research, but their primary role is education and academic publishing. Think tanks focus specifically on producing practical, policy-relevant research quickly, without the slow pace of academic publishing. Some think tanks are attached to universities; others are fully independent.
  • Lobbying firms are hired by companies or interest groups to directly persuade lawmakers to vote a certain way. Think tanks influence policy indirectly — through ideas, research, and public discourse, not through direct paid advocacy.
  • Government agencies (like a planning ministry or a statistics bureau) are part of the government and serve it directly. Think tanks are typically outside government, giving them more freedom to criticize official policy.
  • Consulting firms (like McKinsey or Deloitte) are hired by clients to solve specific problems and produce confidential reports. Think tanks mostly publish their research publicly, so anyone can read it.

• Brookings Institution (USA) — One of the world's most respected think tanks, focusing on economics, governance, and foreign policy. Founded in 1916.
  • RAND Corporation (USA) — Originally set up to advise the U.S. military, now covers everything from health policy to artificial intelligence.
  • Chatham House (UK) — Focuses on international affairs and global security.
  • Council on Foreign Relations (USA) — Specializes in U.S. foreign policy and international relations.
  • Observer Research Foundation (ORF) (India) — One of India's leading think tanks, covering geopolitics, energy, urban development, and digital governance.
  • Centre for Policy Research (CPR) (India) — Focuses on Indian public policy and governance.

Think tanks act as a bridge between the world of raw academic research and the world of real-world decision-making. Politicians and bureaucrats are busy people — they don't always have the time to read hundreds of academic papers. Think tanks translate complex research into clear, actionable recommendations. In this way, they shape government policy, public debate, and even laws.

Think tanks also serve as a repository of expertise. When a new government comes to power, it often draws heavily on the people and ideas from think tanks aligned with its ideology. Many senior politicians, ministers, and advisors once worked at think tanks — and return to them after leaving office.

A think tank is an independent organization of experts who research complex societal, political, or economic problems and publish ideas and recommendations to influence public policy and decision-making.

"Thinly" is the adverb form of "thin." Its job is to describe how something is done — specifically, in a way that involves very little of something: very little thickness, very little density, very little disguise, or very little genuine feeling.

The single idea running through every use of "thinly" is this: barely enough, or not enough at all.
Meaning 1: In a Very Thin Layer

This is the most physical, concrete meaning. When you do something thinly, you apply very little of it, or you cut something into extremely thin pieces.

"Spread the butter thinly on the bread" means use only a small amount and make the layer thin. "Slice the beef thinly" means cut it into very thin slices. "Apply the sunscreen thinly" means don't pile it on — keep the coat light.

The question "thinly" answers here is: how thick is it? The answer: not thick at all.
Meaning 2: Spread Out Sparsely — Not Enough to Fill a Space

Here, "thinly" describes how something is distributed across a large area — people, soldiers, trees, resources. When something is "thinly" distributed, there is not much of it, and it is scattered with wide gaps in between, leaving a lot of empty space.

"The region is thinly populated" means very few people live there — you could travel for miles without seeing a single person. "The army was thinly spread across the border" means there were too few soldiers to properly cover the territory they were responsible for. "Resources were thinly allocated" means there was far too little for the level of need.

The question "thinly" answers here is: how much is there, compared to the space it needs to cover? The answer: not nearly enough — spread too far apart.

This is one of the most common and important uses of the word, and it's worth understanding deeply. Picture draping a thin, almost see-through piece of cloth over an object — you can still clearly see what's underneath. That visual captures exactly what "thinly veiled" or "thinly disguised" means: something is technically hidden or covered, but so poorly that anyone can see straight through it.

"A thinly veiled threat" means the person didn't say the threatening words outright, but the threat was so obvious that no one was fooled. "A thinly disguised attack on her opponent" means the speaker pretended to be talking about something else, but everyone could see it was a direct attack. "Thinly disguised contempt" means someone tried to hide how much they looked down on another person, but failed completely — the contempt was plain on their face or in their words.

The question "thinly" answers here is: how well is it hidden? The answer: barely at all — almost not hidden.
Meaning 4: Weakly, with Very Little Feeling or Conviction

When someone does something "thinly" in this sense, they do it with very little energy, warmth, or genuine feeling — like a pale, hollow version of the real thing.

"She smiled thinly" is perhaps the most classic example of this use. It means she barely smiled — it was a tight, polite, forced, or cold smile with very little warmth behind it. You could tell she wasn't genuinely happy. "He thinly denied the accusations" means his denial was weak and unconvincing — he said the words, but no one believed him. "She argued thinly for the proposal" means her argument lacked depth, strength, and real conviction.

The question "thinly" answers here is: how genuine or strong is it? The answer: barely — weak and hollow.
The One Thread That Ties Everything Together

No matter which meaning you encounter, "thinly" always signals a scarcity — a noticeable lack of something that should be there: thickness, coverage, concealment, or genuine feeling. It always suggests something is barely there, stretched too far, or not quite enough.

Whenever you see "thinly," ask yourself: what is there not enough of here? The answer to that question will unlock the meaning every time.

These are the most common expressions you will encounter in real life with "thinly":

  • Thinly sliced — cut into very thin pieces; most common in food and cooking ("thinly sliced carrots")
  • Thinly spread — distributed across too large an area, with not enough to go around ("resources thinly spread")
  • Thinly populated — describes a place where very few people live ("a thinly populated desert")
  • Thinly veiled — so poorly hidden that it is obvious to everyone ("a thinly veiled insult")
  • Thinly disguised — same idea — a disguise that fools nobody ("thinly disguised jealousy")
  • Smiled thinly — gave a weak, tight, or cold smile with little genuine warmth behind it
